root.meaning: to press, to knead, to massage
root.note: The English word comes from the command form चाँपो (chā̃po), ‘press!’.

stages.meaning: liquid soap for washing your hair

history: Shampoo comes from India and first meant a massage. In Hindi, chā̃po! means ‘press!’, from chā̃pnā, ‘to press, to knead’. British people in India in the 1700s used the word for an Indian-style massage, often in a hot bath. In 1814, Sake Dean Mahomed, a businessman from Patna in India, opened a bath house in Brighton where he offered ‘shampooing’: a steam bath with a massage. It was very popular, and he was later called ‘Shampooing Surgeon’ to King George IV. Only in the 1860s did shampoo get its modern meaning, ‘to wash the hair’, and later it became the name of the soap itself. Pyjamas, bungalow and jungle also came into English from India.
historyEinfach: Shampoo is a word from India. In Hindi, it means ‘press!’. At first, shampoo was a massage. A man from India opened a bath house in Brighton, in England. People loved his ‘shampooing’. About 160 years ago, shampoo started to mean ‘washing your hair’.

elsewhere.text: The Hindi verb mostly means to press or to knead (and to massage), not to wash. English took it for the massage, and only later moved the meaning to hair and soap.
French added -ing to the English word itself: un shampooing is both the liquid and the hair wash. English does not use the word this way. French made un parking and le camping in the same way.
